newsitem.title: UK: Buoyant markets lift British Airways profits.
newsitem.headline: Buoyant markets lift British Airways profits.

text.p: British Airways Plc, Britain's largest airline, Monday announced record profits despite higher prices for jet fuel and said employees would get 10 shares of stock and an average of $2,500 apiece to celebrate the results.

Buoyed by strong growth in air travel worldwide, pretax profit rose 9 percent to 640 million British pounds ($1.05 billion) for the year ended on March 31 while sales rose 8 percent to 8.4 billion pounds ($13.7 billion).
The results came despite a rise in oil prices that pushed up fuel bills 20 percent to 842 million pounds ($1.4 billion).

The formerly state-owned airline also announced it was giving every employee 10 shares of stock to celebrate its 10th anniversary in the private sector. Under a profit-sharing plan, British Airways' 58,200 employees will also receive 89 million pounds ($146 million), or about $2,500 each on average.

Chief Executive Robert Ayling declined to say when he expected to see any movement in the complicated approvals process for its planned affiliation with American Airlines, which had been held up by the British election.
The new Labour government has the task of reviewing the deal in tandem with investigations by the European Union and the U.S. government in Washington.

"I don't expect to hear by any specific date but I think that the momentum is building up again," Ayling told Reuters. The two airlines announced plans last June to coordinate trans-Atlantic services. Some carriers have protested the two carriers would dominate the heavily travelled market.
"It's a very important deal for us and we are not putting a gun to anyone's head with a particular timetable. We are prepared to be patient about this," Ayling said.

Analysts said investors were betting British Airways would eventually win approval for the alliance with American. But a degree of caution was likely to limit gains in its stock, which fell modestly after the report in a lower market in London.
British Airways executives also warned that the strength of the pound could hurt results in the current year. A stronger pound makes revenues earned in other countries worth less in Britain.

"Sterling's current strength will adversely impact profits, although it is anticipated that this will at least partially be offset by lower fuel prices and further business efficiency improvement," Chairman Colin Marshall said.
The company said the unexpected jump in oil prices added 142 million pounds ($233 million) to its fuel costs last year, leading to a drop of 55 million pounds ($90 million) in operating profit.
The results included a one-time charge to cover streamlining measures, almost totally offset by a gain from changes in how it accounted for the investment in its former partner US Airways.
